alignment.note: All three open with a temporal-conjunctive frame, but the discourse particles diverge in placement: Greek pairs ὅταν with postpositive δέ, Syriac splits ܡܐ ('when') from postpositive ܕܝܢ, and the Vulgate prefixes coordinating Et to the temporal cum. The semantic value is equivalent across traditions.

Greek παραδοῖ ('hands over/yields') and Latin produxerit ('brings forth') describe the fruit being produced or offered up, whereas the Peshitta ܕܫܡܢ (root d-sh-m, 'grows fat/ripens') foregrounds the ripeness of the produce. The Syriac thus reads the agronomic process rather than the act of yielding.

Greek ἀποστέλλει and Latin mittit both mean 'he sends (forth) [the sickle]', an active causative idiom for beginning the harvest. The Peshitta ܐܬܝܐ (root a-th-a, 'comes') instead has the sickle 'come', shifting from an external agent dispatching the tool to an impersonal or intransitive arrival, a recognisably Syriac reformulation of the harvest image.
ὅτι / ܕ (relative-causal prefix on ܕܡܛܝ) / quoniam

Greek παρέστηκεν (perfect of παρίστημι, 'has come/stands ready') and Latin adest ('is present') express the harvest standing at hand. The Syriac uses the prefixed verb ܕܡܛܝ (root m-T, 'has arrived/become due'), a cognate idiom for the season having reached its appointed time; the divergence is purely lexical, not semantic.
